design_detail: Brief communication of three case reports from one psychiatric hospital (Lafayette Clinic, Detroit) seen in a single year: three young men with psychoses lasting 2 to 4 weeks after street drugs sold as PCP, THC and methadone, attributed by the authors to phencyclidine on clinical grounds, with their hospital course and treatment.
can_establish: That psychoses lasting weeks, with hostility, disorientation, unsteadiness, insensitivity to pain and later amnesia, were seen after street drugs presumed to contain PCP, and what their course and hospital management looked like in these three men.
cannot_establish: That PCP was taken (no toxicology is reported), how often such prolonged reactions follow PCP, why they happened (dose, metabolism, an underlying psychotic illness or other drugs), or whether any treatment changed the course.

sample.recruitment: Patients admitted to the authors' hospital within one year; cases 1 and 2 came from other doctors' care (the authors thank two colleagues for use of their case material) (p. 1076).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated; cases chosen because the psychoses were unusually long.
sample.demographics: Men aged 19, 18 and 19; case 2 unemployed, case 3 employed (pp. 1076-1077).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; follow-up of one week (case 3) to one month (case 2).
sample.selection_effects: Three striking cases from one hospital, reported because they puzzled the authors; the number of people seen with PCP reactions in that year, and how many recovered within a day, is not given.

exposure.measurement: History only: an anonymous telephone caller told the parents of case 1 that he had taken PCP; case 2 and four friends took a drug sold as THC; case 3 said afterwards he had taken a small pink pill sold as methadone. No blood or urine analysis is reported (pp. 1076-1077). The authors infer PCP from how often street drugs contained it (their own earlier letter) and the clinical picture (p. 1077).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (second-hand reports): case 1 was said to have swallowed a full teaspoon of uncut phencyclidine, described as 5 to 10 times the usual street dose, while packaging a kilogram for resale; amounts unknown in cases 2 and 3; all by mouth as far as reported (pp. 1076-1077).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported; the contents of the street drugs were unknown.

comparison.controls: None. The four friends of case 2, who took the same drug, provide an informal comparison: two were admitted to a detoxification unit and one to a private psychiatric hospital, all discharged within 2 to 3 days (p. 1077).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Previous psychiatric history, family history and earlier drug use are not reported for any of the three; the tests of case 2 at 13 days suggested a chronic schizophrenic process.

outcomes.instruments: Clinical observation and mental state examination; physical examination; for case 2 a psychological test battery (MMPI, Rorschach, Bender-Gestalt, partial WAIS, sentence completion, Gorham Proverbs) at 13 days and a month later (p. 1077).
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis judged clinically; recovery as orientation and absence of psychotic symptoms on interview.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (narrative clinical description without statistics).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Durations: case 1 oriented without psychosis 14 days after the drug; case 2 increasingly aware about 5 days after admission and amnesic for the previous 2 weeks; case 3 psychotic until he left hospital on its 17th day, improving at home (pp. 1076-1077).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable; only three cases described.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Three young men had severe psychoses lasting 2 to 4 weeks after street drugs, with hostility, agitation, disorientation, ataxia, insensitivity to pain or pinprick in one, auditory hallucinations in two, dangerous behaviour, and amnesia for the first two weeks; all recovered, two abruptly, and none had psychosis at follow-up a week to a month later.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors are reasonably certain the men took phencyclidine (p. 1077) and describe a sudden resolution without apparent sequelae; the attribution rests on drug history and clinical signs without toxicology, and the tests of case 2 at 13 days showed residual organic impairment that had improved a month later. They list possible reasons for the long course (dose, slow metabolism, toxic metabolites, idiosyncrasy, an unmasked schizophrenic process) without evidence for any (p. 1078). In case 1, rigid convulsive episodes began the day after the first antipsychotic dose; the authors treat them as PCP convulsions and the paper does not discuss the medicine as a possible contributor, although the parents described similar episodes before transfer.

timeline.event: Greifenstein et al., anaesthesia study cited by the authors: 1 of 65 surgical patients had a stuporous, disoriented state lasting 10 days.
Luby et al., cited by the authors: four people with chronic schizophrenia became acutely psychotic for more than 4 weeks after a small injected dose.
This report of three prolonged psychoses after street drugs presumed to contain PCP; the authors also mention two further prolonged reactions known to them by personal communication.

replication.where_it_stands: An early clinical description, still cited for prolonged PCP psychosis; it shows that such courses occur but gives no rate and no confirmed exposure.

funding.affiliations_note: Wayne State University School of Medicine and Lafayette Clinic, Detroit; Vanderbilt University School of Medicine, Nashville.

what_would_settle_it: Systematic follow-up of people treated for PCP intoxication, with toxicology confirming the drug and recording prior psychiatric history, to count how many have psychosis lasting beyond a few days, and a comparative study of treatments for those who do.

domains.note: Three unusual cases from one hospital in one year, chosen because they were long; no denominator.
No blood or urine testing; the drugs were sold under three different names and PCP was inferred.
An underlying psychotic illness, other drugs and effects of the medicines given are not excluded; previous psychiatric history is not reported.
Course and treatment are described in detail, but there are no laboratory results, histories or longer follow-up.
Internally consistent; the summary of resolution without sequelae is slightly stronger than the improving test results of case 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to case reports (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The report can be cited as a description of what happened to three men and of the authors' attribution and treatment, and as showing that psychoses lasting weeks after presumed PCP were seen. It cannot be cited for how often this happens, for PCP as the confirmed cause, or for the effect of any treatment.

key_findings.finding: Case 1: a 19-year-old man, said by an anonymous caller to have taken PCP, was found wild-eyed and irrational and transferred 4 days later; he was mute, staring, salivating, unable to control his arm position, and insensitive to pinprick. The authors were told he had swallowed a large amount of uncut phencyclidine while packaging it for sale (amount in the exposure field).
key_findings.locator: Case Reports, Case 1 (left column and right column, 1st paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Case 1, course: an antipsychotic (haloperidol) was given 24 hours after the authors first saw him and stopped the next day when he began a series of seizure-like episodes of about 5 minutes with rigidity, arched back and fixed limb postures, tachycardia and sweating; intravenous diphenhydramine did not stop them; his parents reported similar episodes before transfer. He then became assaultive and was secluded; 11 days after the drug he was more cooperative, and 3 days later oriented with no psychotic signs, remembering nothing of the first 2 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Case 1, right column (p. 1076) to the top of the left column (p. 1077)

key_findings.finding: Case 2: an 18-year-old man took a drug sold as THC with four friends; after 20 hours of frantic, erratic behaviour and 30 more hours without sleep he came to the emergency room hostile, suspicious, ataxic, disoriented and hearing chains. Daily chlorpromazine for a week did not change his behaviour; the day after admission he jumped from a third-floor window, landing uninjured. After 4 more days he became more aware, remembering nothing of the previous 2 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Case Reports, Case 2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: Case 2, tests: a psychological battery 13 days after the drug suggested a chronic schizophrenic process with signs of residual organic impairment; a month later there was no evidence of psychosis and the organic impairment had improved. Three of his four friends were hospitalized (two in a detoxification unit, one in a private psychiatric hospital) and discharged within 2 to 3 days.

Case 3: a 19-year-old man, arrested after refusing to answer questions in court, was agitated, heard voices and believed he was being poisoned; in hospital he was ataxic and hostile, walked around nude, thought he was still in jail, and his blood pressure rose from 110/64 to 160/115 on the 16th day. Rising doses of chlorpromazine and trifluoperazine and injected chlorpromazine were not effective; he was calm in a dim, quiet, locked room. On the 17th day he left, collected his pay, had a haircut and went home, where he improved greatly without medication but could not remember what had happened; he later said he had taken a pink pill sold as methadone; an interview a week later found no psychosis or organic brain syndrome.
key_findings.locator: Case Reports, Case 3 (left column, lower part, and right column)

key_findings.finding: Discussion: as cited from earlier literature, PCP's analgesia and anaesthesia usually last 1 to 3 hours, its mind-altering (psychotomimetic) effects 18 to 24 hours and nystagmus and double vision 24 to 36 hours; earlier exceptions were 1 of 65 surgical patients with a 10-day stuporous state and four people with chronic schizophrenia psychotic for more than 4 weeks after a small injected dose.

Treatment, as discussed by the authors: haloperidol or chlorpromazine by injection together with a quiet, isolated environment had been used against PCP's excitatory effects, and haloperidol may work better than the chlorpromazine and trifluoperazine used in cases 2 and 3; haloperidol was not given an adequate trial in case 1 because of his seizures; case 3 became much calmer in a dim, quiet environment.

The authors' grounds for attributing the psychoses to PCP: the history of street drugs often found to contain PCP, and the combination of analgesia, anaesthesia, schizophreniform psychosis, sudden resolution and amnesia, which they say no other drug except possibly ketamine produces; two of the men had excessive salivation and one high blood pressure; no nystagmus was seen.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary says all three men developed analgesia and anaesthesia, and the Discussion uses this as a reason for attributing the psychoses to PCP (pp. 1076-1077), but only case 1 is described as insensitive to pinprick, the report of case 2 mentions no such sign, and the examination of case 3 found no evidence of sensory loss (p. 1077).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the signs used to attribute the psychoses to PCP is documented in only one of the three cases, which weakens the attribution further.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary describes resolution without apparent sequelae, but the tests of case 2, 13 days after the drug, showed residual organic impairment, which a month later had improved rather than been reported as gone.
reporting_issues.consequence: Recovery was described clinically; whether thinking returned fully to normal is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The article begins below the end of another brief communication on the PDF's first page (p. 1076), and the third page continues with a different article; the text layer is OCR from a scan and runs the two columns together.
reporting_issues.consequence: All anchors were checked against rendered page images.
